after.problem: Estimate $\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+\sqrt{y}$ at the point $(8,144).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(8,144),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{1}{3\cdot {8}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{144}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{24}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(8+Δx,144+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{12}\,Δx+\frac{1}{24}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}=f(10,150),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(10,150).$

Moving from $(8,144)$ to $(10,150),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =10-8=2, \\ Δy & =150-144=6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{12}(2)+\frac{1}{24}(6) \\  & ≈\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & ≈\frac{5}{12} \\  & ≈0.417.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.417.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,150) & ≈f(8,144)+0.417 \\ \sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150} & ≈\sqrt[3]{8}+\sqrt{144}+0.417 \\  & ≈2+12+0.417 \\  & ≈14.417.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Estimate $\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ at the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
after.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x-\sqrt{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2\sqrt{4}}\,\text{d}x-\sqrt{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x-2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(4+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx-2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5)=f(3.9,1.5),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3.9,1.5).$

Moving from $(4,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(3.9,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3.9-4=-0.1, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}≈-0.070796.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.1)-2(-0.070796) \\  & ≈0+0.141592 \\  & ≈0.141592.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141592.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.9,1.5) & ≈f(4,\frac{\pi }{2})+0.141592 \\ \sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5) & ≈\sqrt{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+0.141592 \\  & ≈0+0.141592 \\  & ≈0.142,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

content.problem: Estimate $\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ at the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
content.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡y}{2\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x-\sqrt{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(4,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{2\sqrt{4}}\,\text{d}x-\sqrt{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x-2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(4+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx-2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5)=f(3.9,1.5),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3.9,1.5).$

Moving from $(4,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(3.9,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3.9-4=-0.1, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}≈-0.070796.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.1)-2(-0.070796) \\  & ≈0+0.141592 \\  & ≈0.141592.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141592.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3.9,1.5) & ≈f(4,\frac{\pi }{2})+0.141592 \\ \sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5) & ≈\sqrt{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+0.141592 \\  & ≈0+0.141592 \\  & ≈0.142,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

after.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y+\frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,1,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,1,1) & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+1\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,1+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈Δx+Δy+Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,1,1)$ to $(2,3,4),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-1=1, \\ Δy & =3-1=2 \\ Δz & =4-1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈Δx+Δy+Δz \\  & ≈1+2+3 \\  & ≈6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $6.$

after.problem: Given a right triangular prism, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ if the height is $h=5$ and the base is a right triangle with legs $a=4$ and $b=6.$
after.worked_solution:
The volume of a given right triangular prism is $V=\frac{abh}{2}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{bh}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{ah}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{ab}{2}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=4,$ $b=6,$ and $h=5,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(4,6,5) & =\frac{6\cdot 5}{2}\,\text{d}a+\frac{4\cdot 5}{2}\,\text{d}b+\frac{4\cdot 6}{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =15\,\text{d}a+10\text{d}b+12\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$
